categories.name: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks

faults.name: Protruding hardware in the belt path
faults.what: Bolts or fasteners protruding into the carryway or return way; Guards, brackets or frame members intruding into the belt path; Scrapers positioned into the belt path.
conditions: Bolts or fasteners protruding into the carryway or return way
Guards, brackets or frame members intruding into the belt path
Scrapers positioned into the belt path
faults.leads: Belt shaving, scoring, blackening, edge damage, module fracture, exposed rods, belt breakage, downtime and foreign material contamination.
faults.action: Remove the obstruction or countersink the fastener. Replace protruding bolts with hex socket button screws where the belt is not sufficiently contained.
thresholds: Fasteners — Avoid fasteners in the belt path, or keep them out of the path by countersinking
faults.benefit: Belt edges protected and extended belt life.

faults.name: Sharp edges, burrs or rough welds contacting the belt
faults.what: Sharp edges or burrs on frame or components; Rough or proud welds in the belt path; Damaged stainless steel surfaces contacting the belt.
conditions: Sharp edges or burrs on frame or components
Rough or proud welds in the belt path
Damaged stainless steel surfaces contacting the belt
faults.leads: Belt shaving, scoring, blackening, edge damage, module fracture, exposed rods, belt breakage, downtime and foreign material contamination.
faults.action: Grind welds flush in product contact areas and dress all sharp edges. Stainless steel in contact with the belt must be smooth and free of burrs.
thresholds: Welds — Fully weld connections with a minimum 0.125 in (3 mm) radius; grind all welds flush in product contact areas
Stainless finish — 303/304 stainless with a 2B cold-rolled surface finish provides the lowest friction of any stainless carryway
faults.source: ThermoDrive Engineering Manual 5011939.5 (2026); MPB Engineering Manual 5012156.4 (2026)
faults.benefit: Belt edges protected and extended belt life.

faults.name: Wear-strip joints without lead-ins or bevels
faults.what: Wear-strip joints with no chamfer or lead-in; Joint ends oriented so the belt or drive bar catches; Unbevelled transitions between carryway sections.
conditions: Wear-strip joints with no chamfer or lead-in
Joint ends oriented so the belt or drive bar catches
Unbevelled transitions between carryway sections
faults.leads: Belt shaving, scoring, blackening, edge damage, module fracture, exposed rods, belt breakage, downtime and foreign material contamination.
faults.action: Chamfer all rail joints, cut edges and sharp corners to eliminate catch points and allow smooth belt transitions. Chamfer infeed and outfeed ends to prevent drive bar catch points.
thresholds: Chamfer angle — 45 degrees
faults.benefit: Belt edges protected and extended belt life.

faults.name: Debris or abrasive material in the belt path
faults.what: Debris or product trapped beneath the belt; Welding debris or grinding particles embedded in UHMW-PE components; Grit or abrasive material accumulating on the carryway.
conditions: Debris or product trapped beneath the belt
Welding debris or grinding particles embedded in UHMW-PE components
Grit or abrasive material accumulating on the carryway
faults.leads: Belt shaving, scoring, blackening, edge damage, module fracture, exposed rods, belt breakage, downtime and foreign material contamination.
faults.action: Remove trapped debris and replace any UHMW-PE component with embedded abrasive particles. Embedded grit turns a low-friction surface into a cutting surface.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and belt edges protected.

faults.name: Missing, worn or displaced wear strips
faults.what: Wear strips missing over part of the carryway; Wear strips loose, broken or displaced; Heavily worn wear strips; Blackening of the belt surface.
conditions: Wear strips missing over part of the carryway
Wear strips loose, broken or displaced
Heavily worn wear strips
Blackening of the belt surface
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Review and replace all affected wear strips and rollers. Blackening on food contact sides is a product contamination risk; on the underside it wears the belt prematurely and risks breakage.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and extended belt life.

faults.name: Wear-strip configuration unsuitable for the belt or application
faults.what: Pattern not suited to the belt or load; Insufficient number of wear strips for the belt width; Chevron spacing or angle outside recommendation; Belt edges riding over or trapped by wear strips.
conditions: Pattern not suited to the belt or load
Insufficient number of wear strips for the belt width
Chevron spacing or angle outside recommendation
Belt edges riding over or trapped by wear strips
Wear strips interfering with the sprockets
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Reconfigure to a chevron or straight parallel pattern appropriate to the load. A chevron pattern distributes wear more evenly and is the better choice for abrasive or heavily loaded applications.
thresholds: Chevron angle — 20 degrees to 60 degrees
Chevron spacing — Recommended 2 in (51 mm), maximum 5 in (127 mm)
Chevron point gap — Minimum 0.4 in (10 mm) between chevron points
Belt edge clearance — Minimum 0.25 in (6 mm) between belt edge and outer wearstrip
Quantity — Use the Sprocket and Support Quantity Reference table for the selected belt
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and reduced unplanned downtime.

faults.name: Wear-strip joints and thermal expansion not accommodated
faults.what: Joints not staggered across the belt width; No gap left between wear-strip ends; Wear strips fixed without slotted holes; Buckling or lifting of wear strips at temperature.
conditions: Joints not staggered across the belt width
No gap left between wear-strip ends
Wear strips fixed without slotted holes
Buckling or lifting of wear strips at temperature
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Stagger rail joints to minimise drive bar catch points and fix wear strips with plastic bolts and nuts in slotted holes so they can expand and contract with temperature.
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and reduced unplanned downtime.

faults.name: Unsupported carryway spans
faults.what: Belt unsupported between carryway supports; Visible belt deflection under load; Support spacing greater than specification.
conditions: Belt unsupported between carryway supports
Visible belt deflection under load
Support spacing greater than specification
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Reduce the space between adjacent supports to decrease wear-strip load and unsupported belt area.
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and reduced unplanned downtime.

faults.name: No solid support at impact or loading zones
faults.what: Product drop or transfer point with no solid plate beneath the belt; Local belt splitting at an impact point; Wear strips only beneath a high-impact loading area.
conditions: Product drop or transfer point with no solid plate beneath the belt
Local belt splitting at an impact point
Wear strips only beneath a high-impact loading area
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Support impact zones with a solid UHMW-PE carryway plate spanning the conveyor width, with lead-in chamfers so the drive bar does not catch, removable for wash down, and installed to allow thermal expansion.
thresholds: Plate thickness — Greater than 25 mm UHMW-PE
Design principle — Consider using a solid UHMW-PE carryway bed at infeed or loading areas to address product impact
faults.source: ThermoDrive Engineering Manual 5011939.5 (2026); MPB Engineering Manual 5012156.4 (2026)
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and extended belt life.

faults.name: Damaged, seized or misplaced carryway rollers
faults.what: Rollers not turning freely; Flat-spotted or worn-through rollers; Rollers positioned where they do not support the belt.
conditions: Rollers not turning freely
Flat-spotted or worn-through rollers
Rollers positioned where they do not support the belt
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Replace seized or worn rollers and reposition to give even support across the belt width.
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and reduced unplanned downtime.

faults.name: Unsuitable carryway material
faults.what: Acetal or HDPE support rails in use; UHMW-PE in service above its temperature limit; Abrasive or rough carryway surface; Belt surging instead of accelerating smoothly at the infeed.
conditions: Acetal or HDPE support rails in use
UHMW-PE in service above its temperature limit
Abrasive or rough carryway surface
Belt surging instead of accelerating smoothly at the infeed
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Use UHMW-PE for most carryways. Never use acetal or HDPE support rails. Consider slip-stick effect when selecting carryway material.
thresholds: Uhmw pe limit — Suitable up to 160 °F (71 °C); avoid in facility temperatures above this
Nylatron — Usable up to 250 °F (121 °C) but not FDA or USDA-FSIS compliant for direct food contact
Surface finish — Rails with a smooth surface finish not exceeding Ra125 micro-inches (Ra3.2 µm)
Prohibited — Never use acetal or high-density polyethylene (HDPE) support rails
faults.source: ThermoDrive Engineering Manual 5011939.5 (2026); MPB Engineering Manual 5012156.4 (2026)
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and reduced unplanned downtime.

faults.name: ThermoDrive carryway rail geometry out of specification
faults.what: Rails narrower than minimum width; Outermost rails too far from the belt edge; Rail centreline spacing too wide; L-shaped containment rail with insufficient vertical surface.
conditions: Rails narrower than minimum width
Outermost rails too far from the belt edge
Rail centreline spacing too wide
L-shaped containment rail with insufficient vertical surface
faults.leads: Black belt surfaces, linear wear marks, plastic dust or shavings, belt surging, local splitting, uneven wear, increased drive load, rods becoming visible.
faults.action: Set the carryway to specification so the belt tracks correctly and the drive bar does not catch.
thresholds: Rail width min — Flat rails with a minimum 1 in (25 mm) width
Outermost rail to belt edge max — 0.5 in (13 mm)
Rail centreline spacing max — 6.0 in (152 mm)
L rail vertical min — 0.75 in (19 mm) vertical surface on L-shaped containment rails
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and reduced unplanned downtime.

faults.name: Insufficient return-way support
faults.what: Long unsupported spans in the return way; Too few return-way supports for the conveyor length; Return support rollers smaller than minimum diameter.
conditions: Long unsupported spans in the return way
Too few return-way supports for the conveyor length
Return support rollers smaller than minimum diameter
faults.leads: Underside wear, tracking problems, edge damage, unstable catenary sag, poor sprocket engagement, belt shavings and contamination risk.
faults.action: Add return-way support rollers at the specified spacing and diameter.
thresholds: Exemption — End-drive conveyors shorter than 6 ft (1.8 m) usually do not require return-way support, provided sag depth is limited to a maximum of 4 in (102 mm)
Roller diameter min — 2 in (50 mm) for belts up to 1.07 in (27 mm) pitch; 4 in (100 mm) for larger pitch belts
Support spacing — 36 in to 48 in (900 mm to 1,200 mm) apart
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and belt tracks correctly.

faults.name: Damaged, seized or misaligned return rollers
faults.what: Rollers bound up or not turning; Rollers worn through or flat-spotted; Rollers or supports out of level or out of alignment; Wear patterning along the belt length.
conditions: Rollers bound up or not turning
Rollers worn through or flat-spotted
Rollers or supports out of level or out of alignment
Wear patterning along the belt length
faults.leads: Underside wear, tracking problems, edge damage, unstable catenary sag, poor sprocket engagement, belt shavings and contamination risk.
faults.action: Replace with UHMW-PE rollers of the correct diameter and reset to level and alignment. Use solid UHMW-PE rollers without ball bearings for return-way support.
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and belt tracks correctly.

faults.name: Roller or shaft ends contacting the belt
faults.what: Shaft end protruding into the belt path; Roller end or circlip contacting the belt edge; Belt sagging onto a shaft between rollers.
conditions: Shaft end protruding into the belt path
Roller end or circlip contacting the belt edge
Belt sagging onto a shaft between rollers
faults.leads: Underside wear, tracking problems, edge damage, unstable catenary sag, poor sprocket engagement, belt shavings and contamination risk.
faults.action: Space rollers evenly across the belt width and install shaft collars to hold that spacing so the belt cannot sag onto the shaft or protruding fasteners.
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and belt tracks correctly.

faults.name: Flanged rollers missing where containment is required
faults.what: Idle shaft using plain rollers rather than sprockets or flanged rollers; Belt rubbing on the conveyor frame; Premature edge wear on the belt.
conditions: Idle shaft using plain rollers rather than sprockets or flanged rollers
Belt rubbing on the conveyor frame
Premature edge wear on the belt
faults.leads: Underside wear, tracking problems, edge damage, unstable catenary sag, poor sprocket engagement, belt shavings and contamination risk.
faults.action: Where idle rollers are used rather than sprockets, use flanged rollers to track the belt correctly. Any containment disk should match the flanged roller dimensions.
thresholds: Flange clearance — Dimension A greater than the height of the belt (S2400: 12.7 mm + chamfer height)
Material — UHMW-PE
Flange height — 0.5 in (12.7 mm)
Max flanged roller diameter — 5 in (127 mm) and 7 in (178 mm)
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and belt tracks correctly.

faults.name: Catenary sag contacting equipment or structure
faults.what: Belt sag touching the floor; Sag contacting drip pans, brackets, guarding or wiring; Drip pans positioned too close to the belt; Cross members positioned where a loose belt sags onto them.
conditions: Belt sag touching the floor
Sag contacting drip pans, brackets, guarding or wiring
Drip pans positioned too close to the belt
Cross members positioned where a loose belt sags onto them
faults.leads: Underside wear, tracking problems, edge damage, unstable catenary sag, poor sprocket engagement, belt shavings and contamination risk.
faults.action: Choose a belt length and support layout that prevents belt contact with obstacles, and locate cross members under the return-way belt supports.
thresholds: thermodrive clearance by open span: Up to 2 ft 0.61 m — 4.0 in (102 mm)
thermodrive clearance by open span: 3 ft 0.91 m — 6.0 in (152 mm)
thermodrive clearance by open span: 4 ft 1.22 m — 9.0 in (229 mm)
thermodrive clearance by open span: 5 ft 1.52 m — 12.0 in (305 mm)
thermodrive clearance by open span: 6 ft 1.83 m — 15.0 in (381 mm)
Accessories — For belts with flights or sidewalls, add the height of the tallest accessory to the clearance needed
faults.benefit: Extended belt life and belt tracks correctly.

faults.name: Inadequate access for cleaning and inspection
faults.what: Return way cannot be reached for cleaning; Components under the carryway not accessible for inspection; No belt lifting or idle shaft removal mechanism.
conditions: Return way cannot be reached for cleaning
Components under the carryway not accessible for inspection
No belt lifting or idle shaft removal mechanism
faults.leads: Underside wear, tracking problems, edge damage, unstable catenary sag, poor sprocket engagement, belt shavings and contamination risk.
faults.action: Install simple belt lifting and idle shaft removal mechanisms and ensure access to all frame components under the belt for cleaning, sanitation and inspection.
thresholds: Floor to product contact surface min — 18 in (457 mm)
Floor to lower frame min — 12 in (305 mm)
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and extended belt life.

faults.name: Excessive catenary sag
faults.what: First sag section deeper than specification; Belt jumping teeth at the drive; Sag increasing progressively along the return way.
conditions: First sag section deeper than specification
Belt jumping teeth at the drive
Sag increasing progressively along the return way
faults.leads: Poor sprocket engagement, belt jumping, vibration, mistracking, accelerated wear, excessive shaft loading and belt failure.
faults.action: Reduce sag depth to restore back tension. Additional catenary sag decreases belt tension and can lead to sprocket disengagement. Back tension increases as the sag section length increases and as sag depth decreases.
thresholds: Sag depth — 1 in to 4 in (25 mm to 102 mm) for each catenary sag section, including the first section after the snub support
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Insufficient sag or over-tensioned belt
faults.what: No visible catenary in the return way; Belt taut between shafts; High drive load with no other cause.
conditions: No visible catenary in the return way
Belt taut between shafts
High drive load with no other cause
faults.leads: Poor sprocket engagement, belt jumping, vibration, mistracking, accelerated wear, excessive shaft loading and belt failure.
faults.action: Provide sag storage to accommodate temporary belt length changes. For ThermoDrive, verify tensionless operation by stopping the conveyor and shifting the belt sideways at the infeed idle end — it should move with minimal effort.
thresholds: Thermodrive principle — Never operate ThermoDrive belting with tension
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Snub support missing, mispositioned or not engaged
faults.what: No snub support roller fitted; Snub roller not in contact with the belt; Snub roller too far from the shaft; Insufficient belt wrap around the sprockets.
conditions: No snub support roller fitted
Snub roller not in contact with the belt
Snub roller too far from the shaft
Insufficient belt wrap around the sprockets
faults.leads: Poor sprocket engagement, belt jumping, vibration, mistracking, accelerated wear, excessive shaft loading and belt failure.
faults.action: Position the snub support roller so the belt wraps correctly around the sprockets and the first catenary sag section can generate back tension.
thresholds: Snub distance from shaft — 9 in to 18 in (229 mm to 457 mm) from the drive and idle shafts
Belt wrap — Between 180 degrees and 210 degrees around the sprockets
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Return support spacing incorrect
faults.what: Supports too far apart; Supports too close together to allow storage; Uneven spacing along the return way.
conditions: Supports too far apart
Supports too close together to allow storage
Uneven spacing along the return way
faults.leads: Poor sprocket engagement, belt jumping, vibration, mistracking, accelerated wear, excessive shaft loading and belt failure.
faults.action: Set return-way support spacing to specification. This distance combines with the first sag section depth and the shaft-to-snub distance to provide the tension required for proper sprocket engagement.
thresholds: Modular belt — 36 in to 48 in (900 mm to 1,200 mm) apart. Certain belt series require different spacing — see Alternative Returnway Support Spacing.
Thermodrive — Include at least one open span between 30 in (762 mm) and 72 in (1,829 mm) in most applications, positioned where deep sag is wanted
faults.source: MPB Engineering Manual 5012156.4 (2026); ThermoDrive Engineering Manual 5011939.5 (2026)
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Break-in period not monitored
faults.what: Newly installed belt developing excessive sag; No record of pitch or sag measurement since installation; Belt not shortened after break-in.
conditions: Newly installed belt developing excessive sag
No record of pitch or sag measurement since installation
Belt not shortened after break-in
faults.leads: Poor sprocket engagement, belt jumping, vibration, mistracking, accelerated wear, excessive shaft loading and belt failure.
faults.action: Measure catenary sag and belt pitch frequently through the break-in period, which occurs during the first several days to weeks of operation. If elongation is excessive, remove two rows of modules — two rows preserves bricklay pattern integrity and strength.
thresholds: Expected growth — 0.5% to 1% of total length
Correction — Remove two rows of modules
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Take-up causing overtension or shaft misalignment
faults.what: Screw take-up wound in unevenly side to side; Take-up used to remove all sag; Shafts pulled out of parallel by the take-up.
conditions: Screw take-up wound in unevenly side to side
Take-up used to remove all sag
Shafts pulled out of parallel by the take-up
faults.leads: Poor sprocket engagement, belt jumping, vibration, mistracking, accelerated wear, excessive shaft loading and belt failure.
faults.action: Use a take-up only where catenary sag alone does not provide adequate back tension, and adjust both sides equally to keep shafts parallel.
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Inadequate belt storage for expansion and wear growth
faults.what: No allowance for thermal expansion in the belt length; Sag disappearing at operating temperature; Sag bottoming out at maximum load.
conditions: No allowance for thermal expansion in the belt length
Sag disappearing at operating temperature
Sag bottoming out at maximum load
faults.leads: Poor sprocket engagement, belt jumping, vibration, mistracking, accelerated wear, excessive shaft loading and belt failure.
faults.action: Size the belt and return-way layout for the full range of expected length change from load, temperature and wear. Intralox assumes an average ambient temperature of about 70 °F (21 °C).
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Sprocket retainers missing, displaced or on the wrong sprocket
faults.what: No retainer rings fitted; Retainers loose or moved along the shaft; The wrong sprocket locked in place; All sprockets locked, preventing lateral float.
conditions: No retainer rings fitted
Retainers loose or moved along the shaft
The wrong sprocket locked in place
All sprockets locked, preventing lateral float
faults.leads: Uneven belt loading, linear breakage, tooth jumping, mistracking, accelerated sprocket and hinge wear, edge damage and unexpected belt failure.
faults.action: Lock the centre sprocket. If only two sprockets are used, lock the sprocket on the drive journal side. All other sprockets must be free to move laterally as the belt expands and contracts. Where the belt is removed frequently for wash down, use sprocket spacers.
thresholds: Groove caution — Spring-type rings require grooves cut into the shaft corners, which concentrate stress. Where belt pull is high, use Self-Set or Split Collar rings that require no grooves — see Belt Pull Limits vs Shaft Span for Retainer Ring Grooves.
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Worn, damaged or contaminated sprockets
faults.what: Tooth profile visibly worn; Chipped or cracked sprocket teeth; Product or debris packed into the sprocket pockets.
conditions: Tooth profile visibly worn
Chipped or cracked sprocket teeth
Product or debris packed into the sprocket pockets
faults.leads: Uneven belt loading, linear breakage, tooth jumping, mistracking, accelerated sprocket and hinge wear, edge damage and unexpected belt failure.
faults.action: Replace worn sprockets. Sprocket replacement at the time of belt replacement is strongly recommended.
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Sprocket timing incorrect on square shafts
faults.what: Alignment notches or holes not on the same side of the shaft; Uneven engagement across the belt width; Belt bounce at the drive.
conditions: Alignment notches or holes not on the same side of the shaft
Uneven engagement across the belt width
Belt bounce at the drive
faults.leads: Uneven belt loading, linear breakage, tooth jumping, mistracking, accelerated sprocket and hinge wear, edge damage and unexpected belt failure.
faults.action: When installing sprockets with a number of teeth not evenly divisible by 4 on a square shaft, align the notches or holes on the same side of the shaft.
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Incorrect sprocket quantity or distribution
faults.what: Too few sprockets for the belt width and load; Uneven distribution across the shaft; Unsupported belt edge at the drive.
conditions: Too few sprockets for the belt width and load
Uneven distribution across the shaft
Unsupported belt edge at the drive
faults.leads: Uneven belt loading, linear breakage, tooth jumping, mistracking, accelerated sprocket and hinge wear, edge damage and unexpected belt failure.
faults.action: Set sprocket quantity and spacing from the Sprocket and Support Quantity Reference table for the selected belt, and distribute evenly across the shaft.
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Mixed sprocket sizes, types or wear states on one shaft
faults.what: Different sprocket types on the same shaft; New and heavily worn sprockets mixed; Different pitch diameters on one shaft.
conditions: Different sprocket types on the same shaft
New and heavily worn sprockets mixed
Different pitch diameters on one shaft
faults.leads: Uneven belt loading, linear breakage, tooth jumping, mistracking, accelerated sprocket and hinge wear, edge damage and unexpected belt failure.
faults.action: Replace as a set so that engagement is even across the belt width. Mixed wear states load the belt unevenly and can cause linear breakage.
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Bent, non-parallel or excessively deflecting shafts
faults.what: Drive and idle shafts not parallel; Visible shaft deflection under load; Bent shaft or damaged journal.
conditions: Drive and idle shafts not parallel
Visible shaft deflection under load
Bent shaft or damaged journal
faults.leads: Uneven belt loading, linear breakage, tooth jumping, mistracking, accelerated sprocket and hinge wear, edge damage and unexpected belt failure.
faults.action: Correct shaft alignment and confirm shaft size is adequate for the adjusted belt pull. Excessive deflection causes uneven engagement and accelerates hinge and sprocket wear.
thresholds: Max deflection — Recommended maximum 0.10 in (2.5 mm) for standard shafts
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Poor drive engagement or insufficient belt wrap
faults.what: Belt jumping teeth under load; Audible clicking at the drive; Insufficient wrap angle at the drive sprockets.
conditions: Belt jumping teeth under load
Audible clicking at the drive
Insufficient wrap angle at the drive sprockets
faults.leads: Uneven belt loading, linear breakage, tooth jumping, mistracking, accelerated sprocket and hinge wear, edge damage and unexpected belt failure.
faults.action: Restore back tension and belt wrap. Confirm sprockets are aligned with the carryway and belt path before replacing components.
faults.benefit: Reliable sprocket engagement and extended belt life.

faults.name: Belt rubbing continuously against the frame
faults.what: Belt contacting side frames, flanges or roller hangers; Polished wear marks on the frame; Plastic dust accumulating along one side.
conditions: Belt contacting side frames, flanges or roller hangers
Polished wear marks on the frame
Plastic dust accumulating along one side
faults.leads: Edge shaving, uneven wear, belt climbing, damaged modules, increased friction, high drive load, contamination and belt failure.
faults.action: Correct the tracking cause rather than the symptom. Check locked sprocket position, frame squareness and shaft parallelism before replacing the belt.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and belt tracks correctly.

faults.name: Frame not square or shafts not parallel
faults.what: Conveyor frame out of square; Drive and idle shafts not parallel; Belt consistently drifting to one side.
conditions: Conveyor frame out of square
Drive and idle shafts not parallel
Belt consistently drifting to one side
faults.leads: Edge shaving, uneven wear, belt climbing, damaged modules, increased friction, high drive load, contamination and belt failure.
faults.action: Square the frame and set the shafts parallel. This is the root cause behind most persistent tracking problems and it will not be fixed by a new belt.
faults.benefit: Belt tracks correctly and belt edges protected.

faults.name: Side containment too tight, sharp or without expansion clearance
faults.what: Containment forcing the belt edge upward or inward; Sharp transitions in the containment line; No side clearance for thermal expansion; Belt climbing over the containment.
conditions: Containment forcing the belt edge upward or inward
Sharp transitions in the containment line
No side clearance for thermal expansion
Belt climbing over the containment
faults.leads: Edge shaving, uneven wear, belt climbing, damaged modules, increased friction, high drive load, contamination and belt failure.
faults.action: Set containment with smooth transitions and clearance for the belt to expand. Calculate the full range of minimum and maximum belt dimensions before setting containment.
faults.benefit: Belt tracks correctly and belt edges protected.

faults.name: Worn belt containment guides
faults.what: Significant play in the containment guides; Guide surface worn through; Belt wandering within the containment.
conditions: Significant play in the containment guides
Guide surface worn through
Belt wandering within the containment
faults.leads: Edge shaving, uneven wear, belt climbing, damaged modules, increased friction, high drive load, contamination and belt failure.
faults.action: Replace the guides or move the belt to a less worn section of guide. ThermoDrive belting relies on edge containment for tracking; without it the belt will wander and suffer premature damage.
faults.benefit: Belt tracks correctly and belt edges protected.

faults.name: Radius wear strips misaligned or incorrectly profiled
faults.what: Radius wear strips out of alignment through the turn; Incorrect profile at the inside or outside edge; Belt edge catching at the wear-strip infeed.
conditions: Radius wear strips out of alignment through the turn
Incorrect profile at the inside or outside edge
Belt edge catching at the wear-strip infeed
faults.leads: Edge shaving, uneven wear, belt climbing, damaged modules, increased friction, high drive load, contamination and belt failure.
faults.action: Realign and profile the radius wear strips so the belt edge is supported through the turn and cannot catch at the infeed.
faults.benefit: Belt tracks correctly and belt edges protected.

faults.name: Belt reinstalled incorrectly after cleaning
faults.what: Belt installed upside down; Belt installed against the preferred running direction; Rods reinserted from the wrong side.
conditions: Belt installed upside down
Belt installed against the preferred running direction
Rods reinserted from the wrong side
faults.leads: Edge shaving, uneven wear, belt climbing, damaged modules, increased friction, high drive load, contamination and belt failure.
faults.action: Confirm orientation against the moulded direction cues before returning the conveyor to service, and include belt orientation in the post-sanitation check.
faults.benefit: Belt tracks correctly and belt edges protected.

faults.name: Cracked, split, gouged or missing modules
faults.what: Modules cracked or split; Modules gouged or bent; Modules missing from the belt; Local splitting at an impact point.
conditions: Modules cracked or split
Modules gouged or bent
Modules missing from the belt
Local splitting at an impact point
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace affected modules or the belt. Identify and correct the cause — impact, catch point or material selection — before returning to service.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Damaged or heavily worn belt edges
faults.what: Edge modules broken or missing; Edge shaving or scalloping; Edge failure in multiple sections; Premature edge wear on one side only.
conditions: Edge modules broken or missing
Edge shaving or scalloping
Edge failure in multiple sections
Premature edge wear on one side only
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace the affected sections and correct the cause. Edge damage is a symptom — the cause is usually tracking, containment, a catch point or running direction.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Hinge rod damage, protrusion or retention failure
faults.what: Rods loose or migrating; Rods protruding beyond the belt edge; Rod retention features failed or incorrectly installed; Rods damaged or missing.
conditions: Rods loose or migrating
Rods protruding beyond the belt edge
Rod retention features failed or incorrectly installed
Rods damaged or missing
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace affected rows and confirm the rod retention feature is correctly installed. A migrating rod is a foreign material event waiting to happen.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Exposed rods from underside wear
faults.what: Rod ends visible through worn module underside; Belt underside worn to the rod line; Wear concentrated over narrow wear strips.
conditions: Rod ends visible through worn module underside
Belt underside worn to the rod line
Wear concentrated over narrow wear strips
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace the belt and correct the support that caused the wear pattern before installing the new one.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Mixed materials or incompatible replacement modules
faults.what: Patchwork of acetal and polypropylene in one belt; Replacement modules not matching the original specification; Mixed rod materials through the belt.
conditions: Patchwork of acetal and polypropylene in one belt
Replacement modules not matching the original specification
Mixed rod materials through the belt
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace the belt to a single specification. Mixed materials have different strength, thermal expansion and chemical resistance, so the belt fails at the boundary.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and reduced foreign material contamination risk.

faults.name: Improper or temporary field repairs still in service
faults.what: Sections welded or spliced in from a different belt style; Temporary repair left in production; Non-standard fasteners used to join modules.
conditions: Sections welded or spliced in from a different belt style
Temporary repair left in production
Non-standard fasteners used to join modules
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace the repaired section to specification. Record how long the temporary repair has been in service.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Delamination or end of food-safe life
faults.what: Delamination in the centre or edge of the belt; Surface no longer cleanable; Ingrained soiling that does not respond to sanitation.
conditions: Delamination in the centre or edge of the belt
Surface no longer cleanable
Ingrained soiling that does not respond to sanitation
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace the belt. A surface that cannot be cleaned is a sanitation risk regardless of remaining mechanical life.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and reduced foreign material contamination risk.

faults.name: Pitch elongation or belt stretch
faults.what: Increased gap in the hinge area; Measured elongation approaching the replacement rule of thumb; Increased belt bounce at the drive; Camshaft-style wear on the hinge rods.
conditions: Increased gap in the hinge area
Measured elongation approaching the replacement rule of thumb
Increased belt bounce at the drive
Camshaft-style wear on the hinge rods
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Measure over a stated row count and record the span. Where within acceptable range, monitor closely for change; significant length change results in sprocket disengagement.
thresholds: Replacement guidance — Replacement recommended at 3% elongation
Replacement guidance note — Intralox technical team rule of thumb, not a published specification. Do not present to a customer as a manufacturer spec.
Measurement method — Measure over a stated number of rows and record the span (e.g. 10 rows: 520 mm)
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and reduced foreign material contamination risk.

faults.name: Plastic shavings, dust or discoloured wear debris
faults.what: Plastic dust or shavings beneath the conveyor; Discoloured wear debris on the frame; Fragments collecting in the return way.
conditions: Plastic dust or shavings beneath the conveyor
Discoloured wear debris on the frame
Fragments collecting in the return way
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Trace the debris to its source before cleaning it up — the location of the shavings identifies the contact point that is generating them.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Chemical attack on belt or components
faults.what: Swelling or softening of modules; Brittleness or cracking without mechanical cause; Discolouration of belt or rods; Attack concentrated at a chemical application point.
conditions: Swelling or softening of modules
Brittleness or cracking without mechanical cause
Discolouration of belt or rods
Attack concentrated at a chemical application point
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Identify the chemical and confirm compatibility against the Chemical Resistance Guide before specifying a replacement material.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and reduced foreign material contamination risk.

faults.name: Accessories damaged or separating
faults.what: Flights damaged along the belt length; Sideguards separating from the base belt; Tabs or other accessories cracked or missing.
conditions: Flights damaged along the belt length
Sideguards separating from the base belt
Tabs or other accessories cracked or missing
faults.leads: Foreign material contamination, loss of product control, reduced belt strength, secondary conveyor damage and sudden belt failure.
faults.action: Replace affected accessories and confirm they are adequately supported through the carryway and transitions.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Belt material outside its temperature range
faults.what: Operating temperature above the material's upper limit; Operating temperature below the material's lower limit; Polypropylene in high-impact service in a chilled area; Brittle fracture with no mechanical cause.
conditions: Operating temperature above the material's upper limit
Operating temperature below the material's lower limit
Polypropylene in high-impact service in a chilled area
Brittle fracture with no mechanical cause
faults.action: Confirm the measured operating temperature against the material range and reselect if outside. Polypropylene is relatively strong in normal use but becomes somewhat brittle at low temperatures; acetal is considerably stronger than polypropylene and polyethylene.
thresholds: PP: Range — 34 °F to 220 °F (1 °C to 104 °C)
PP: Caution — Not recommended in high-impact conditions below 45 °F (7 °C)
PE: Range — -100 °F to 150 °F (-73 °C to 66 °C)
PE: Note — For exact temperatures see the belt data table for the selected belt style
AC: Range — -50 °F to 200 °F (-46 °C to 93 °C)
PK: Range — -40 °F to 176 °F (-40 °C to 80 °C)
AR nylon: Range — -50 °F to 240 °F (-46 °C to 116 °C)
detectable acetal: Range — -50 °F to 200 °F (-46 °C to 93 °C)
detectable acetal: Caution — Good impact resistance above 34 °F (1 °C)
detectable PP A22: Range — 0 °F to 150 °F (-18 °C to 66 °C)
detectable PP A22: Caution — Good impact resistance above 34 °F (1 °C)
ChemBlox: Range — 0 °F to 150 °F (-18 °C to 66 °C)
PVDF: Range — 34 °F to 200 °F (1 °C to 93 °C)
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Chemical incompatibility with process or sanitation chemicals
faults.what: Belt or rod material not rated for the sanitation chemistry; Peracetic acid or similar in continuous contact; Chemical change of belt properties observed.
conditions: Belt or rod material not rated for the sanitation chemistry
Peracetic acid or similar in continuous contact
Chemical change of belt properties observed
faults.action: Confirm belt and rod material against the Chemical Resistance Guide for the actual process and cleaning chemicals in use.
thresholds: Warning — Do not passivate with nitric acid with any ThermoDrive or other Intralox belt present in the room — nitric acid passivation destroys Intralox polymer belts
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Insufficient belt strength for the application
faults.what: Belt pull exceeding the belt's rating; Conveyor length, incline or load beyond the original design; Application changed since the belt was specified.
conditions: Belt pull exceeding the belt's rating
Conveyor length, incline or load beyond the original design
Application changed since the belt was specified
faults.action: Recalculate belt pull for the current load, length, incline, speed, temperature and service duty. Do not assume the original selection still applies if the application has changed.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Rod material inappropriate for the application
faults.what: Rod material not matched to the belt material; Rod material not rated for the temperature or chemistry; Non-detectable rods where detectable material is required.
conditions: Rod material not matched to the belt material
Rod material not rated for the temperature or chemistry
Non-detectable rods where detectable material is required
faults.action: Specify rod material to match the application, not just the belt. In dry environments, use PK or acetal rods rather than X-ray detectable PK rods.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and unplanned belt failure avoided.

faults.name: Speed, load, impact or abrasion beyond application limits
faults.what: Belt speed increased since original specification; Product load higher than design; Repeated concentrated impact; Abrasive product or environment.
conditions: Belt speed increased since original specification
Product load higher than design
Repeated concentrated impact
Abrasive product or environment
faults.action: Record the actual operating conditions and compare against the original selection. High-speed operation introduces belt whipping and other dynamic effects not present at design speed.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Belt style unsuitable for the duty
faults.what: Style unsuited to the product being conveyed; Insufficient drainage or open area; Style unsuited to the transfer requirement; Style difficult to clean for the hygiene requirement.
conditions: Style unsuited to the product being conveyed
Insufficient drainage or open area
Style unsuited to the transfer requirement
Style difficult to clean for the hygiene requirement
Friction top worn or inadequate for the incline
faults.action: Reselect the belt style against the actual duty — product, drainage, impact, transfer and cleaning requirement.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Unsupported flights, sideguards or raised features
faults.what: Flights unsupported through the carryway; Sideguards without support through transitions; Raised features catching on fixed components.
conditions: Flights unsupported through the carryway
Sideguards without support through transitions
Raised features catching on fixed components
faults.action: Provide support for raised features through the carryway and transitions, and allow for accessory height when setting return-way clearances.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Belt bending tighter than minimum backbend radius
faults.what: Transition, roller or wheel below the minimum bend radius; Belt reverse-bending over a small component; Cracking at the hinge on the return way.
conditions: Transition, roller or wheel below the minimum bend radius
Belt reverse-bending over a small component
Cracking at the hinge on the return way
faults.action: Ensure all transitions, rollers, wheels and sprockets are at or above the minimum bend radius for the belt, including any synchronised sidewalls.
thresholds: Reference — See the belt data tables in Product Line for minimum bend radius
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Radius belt running in the non-preferred direction
faults.what: Flat turning application running against the preferred direction; Edge modules opening outwards through the turn; Edge damage concentrated at the wear-strip infeed.
conditions: Flat turning application running against the preferred direction
Edge modules opening outwards through the turn
Edge damage concentrated at the wear-strip infeed
faults.action: Run flat turning applications in the preferred direction so that under load the edge modules do not open outwards where they can catch on catch points and wear-strip infeeds.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Replacement parts not matching original specification
faults.what: Replacement modules of a different material or style; Sprockets substituted with a different type; Rollers or wear strips substituted with unsuitable material.
conditions: Replacement modules of a different material or style
Sprockets substituted with a different type
Rollers or wear strips substituted with unsuitable material
faults.action: Specify replacements to the original belt and component specification, or requalify the change deliberately.
faults.benefit: Unplanned belt failure avoided and extended belt life.

faults.name: Excessive gap between conveyors
faults.what: Large gap at the transfer; Product tipping or falling into the gap; Small product requiring a tighter transfer than the sprocket allows.
conditions: Large gap at the transfer
Product tipping or falling into the gap
Small product requiring a tighter transfer than the sprocket allows
faults.action: Reduce the transfer gap, or use a smaller pitch diameter or nosebar transfer where a tight transfer is required.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Dead plate or transfer surface incorrectly set
faults.what: Dead plate positioned too high or too low; Transfer surface above or below the belt surface; Dead plate not adjusted after belt replacement.
conditions: Dead plate positioned too high or too low
Transfer surface above or below the belt surface
Dead plate not adjusted after belt replacement
faults.action: Set transfer surfaces flush with or marginally below the belt surface so product does not catch and the belt does not run against the plate.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Transfer components contacting the belt
faults.what: Dead plate, nosebar or transfer roller rubbing the belt; Sharp edges on transfer components; Inadequate lead-ins at the transfer.
conditions: Dead plate, nosebar or transfer roller rubbing the belt
Sharp edges on transfer components
Inadequate lead-ins at the transfer
faults.action: Set clearance and add lead-in chamfers so the belt and drive bar cannot catch on the transfer component.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Large sprocket or roller where a small transfer is required
faults.what: Product tipping over the transfer; Sprocket pitch diameter too large for the product; Significant drop between decline and the following belt.
conditions: Product tipping over the transfer
Sprocket pitch diameter too large for the product
Significant drop between decline and the following belt
faults.action: Use a smaller pitch diameter, a nosebar or a transfer roller sized to the product being handled.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Product trapping, tipping, jamming or falling at the transfer
faults.what: Product jamming at the transfer; Product falling between conveyors; Product tipping and requiring operator intervention.
conditions: Product jamming at the transfer
Product falling between conveyors
Product tipping and requiring operator intervention
faults.action: Correct the transfer geometry. Record the throughput and yield impact, since this is usually the loss the customer feels first.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Product loading creating concentrated or repeated impact
faults.what: Product dropping onto the belt from height; Loading concentrated on a narrow band of the belt; Belt damage localised at the loading point.
conditions: Product dropping onto the belt from height
Loading concentrated on a narrow band of the belt
Belt damage localised at the loading point
faults.action: Reduce drop height or spread the loading point, and support the impact zone with a solid carryway plate.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Scrapers, guides, chutes or diverters incorrectly positioned
faults.what: Scraper bearing too hard on the belt; Guide rails forcing product against the belt edge; Chute or diverter contacting the belt.
conditions: Scraper bearing too hard on the belt
Guide rails forcing product against the belt edge
Chute or diverter contacting the belt
faults.action: Reset positions and pressures. Plan to use position limiters with any scraper.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Unstable product flow causing surges or excessive loading
faults.what: Product arriving in surges; Accumulation causing intermittent high belt load; Line speed mismatch between conveyors.
conditions: Product arriving in surges
Accumulation causing intermittent high belt load
Line speed mismatch between conveyors
faults.action: Address the flow upstream. Surge loading produces belt pull peaks well above the calculated steady-state figure.
faults.benefit: Throughput restored and less operator intervention.

faults.name: Component shavings entering the product stream
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Belt, wear-strip, roller or sprocket shavings above open product; Plastic dust generated over a product zone; Shavings found in product or on the food contact surface.
conditions: Belt, wear-strip, roller or sprocket shavings above open product
Plastic dust generated over a product zone
Shavings found in product or on the food contact surface
faults.action: Stop and isolate the conveyor where site procedures require it, contain affected product, and correct the generating contact point before restart.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Blackened belt surface transferring to product
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Blackening on the food contact side; Black marking transferring onto product; Blackening on the underside with product exposure below.
conditions: Blackening on the food contact side
Black marking transferring onto product
Blackening on the underside with product exposure below
faults.action: Review and replace the wear strips and rollers generating the blackening, and assess whether affected product requires containment.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Cracked, fragmented or missing plastic components over product
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Missing module, flight or tab over open product; Fragments of plastic unaccounted for; Cracked component at risk of shedding.
conditions: Missing module, flight or tab over open product
Fragments of plastic unaccounted for
Cracked component at risk of shedding
faults.action: Account for the missing material. Where a fragment cannot be located, treat as a foreign material event under the site procedure.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Makeshift repairs near exposed product
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Cable ties, wire or tape in or near the product zone; Temporary fasteners holding a component in place; Non-food-grade material used in a repair.
conditions: Cable ties, wire or tape in or near the product zone
Temporary fasteners holding a component in place
Non-food-grade material used in a repair
faults.action: Remove and replace with a permanent, food-safe repair. Record how long the temporary repair has been in place.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Hollow or damaged framework collecting product and moisture
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Open or unsealed hollow sections; Framework drilled or tapped without sealing; Niches, butt joints or lap joints holding product; Frame showing pitting or cracking.
conditions: Open or unsealed hollow sections
Framework drilled or tapped without sealing
Niches, butt joints or lap joints holding product
Frame showing pitting or cracking
faults.action: Seal or replace. Avoid tapping or drilling hollow frame components; use standoffs where hermetically sealed joints are not possible, and eliminate exposed threads, niches, butt joints and lap joints.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Standing water or blocked drainage
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Water pooling on the frame or in drip pans; Drainage blocked or absent; Flat surfaces with no slope to drain.
conditions: Water pooling on the frame or in drip pans
Drainage blocked or absent
Flat surfaces with no slope to drain
faults.action: Clear or redesign the drainage. Slope flat top surfaces so they drain rather than hold water.
thresholds: Portable conveyor top plate slope — 0.125–0.250 in (3.2–6.4 mm)
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Drip pans inaccessible or uncleanable
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Drip pan cannot be removed for cleaning; Drip pan cannot be inspected in place; Drip pan positioned where the belt contacts it.
conditions: Drip pan cannot be removed for cleaning
Drip pan cannot be inspected in place
Drip pan positioned where the belt contacts it
faults.action: Make drip pans removable and inspectable, and reposition clear of the belt sag envelope.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Components concealed beneath the carryway and excluded from inspection
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Components under the carryway not on any inspection routine; Areas that cannot be seen without dismantling; Soiling found in areas not previously inspected.
conditions: Components under the carryway not on any inspection routine
Areas that cannot be seen without dismantling
Soiling found in areas not previously inspected
faults.action: Add these areas to the routine inspection scope and provide access. Keep structures simple to allow open access to all areas during sanitation.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Metal particles, weld spatter or grit embedded in plastic components
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Grinding particles embedded in UHMW-PE; Weld spatter on or in the belt path; Grit embedded in wear strips or rollers.
conditions: Grinding particles embedded in UHMW-PE
Weld spatter on or in the belt path
Grit embedded in wear strips or rollers
faults.action: Replace the contaminated component. Embedded metal turns a wear surface into an abrasive and is a direct foreign material source.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Components that cannot be removed or accessed for sanitation
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Components requiring tools and extended downtime to clean; Belt cannot be lifted for return-way cleaning; Guarding preventing sanitation access.
conditions: Components requiring tools and extended downtime to clean
Belt cannot be lifted for return-way cleaning
Guarding preventing sanitation access
faults.action: Provide tool-free or simple-access removal for components in the sanitation scope.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Non-detectable parts where detectable material is required
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Non-detectable replacement modules in a detectable-belt application; Non-detectable rods in a detectable belt; Component material not matching the plant risk assessment.
conditions: Non-detectable replacement modules in a detectable-belt application
Non-detectable rods in a detectable belt
Component material not matching the plant risk assessment
faults.action: Replace to the material specified by the plant risk assessment. Test the material in the plant's own detector — detection sensitivity is best determined in the production environment.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Loose hardware or component fragments over exposed product
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Loose fasteners above the product zone; Unsecured hardware on guarding or framework; Fragments found on the conveyor above product.
conditions: Loose fasteners above the product zone
Unsecured hardware on guarding or framework
Fragments found on the conveyor above product
faults.action: Secure or remove. Anything above open product that can fall is a critical finding regardless of its condition.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.

faults.name: Leaking seals, bearings or gearboxes over product zones
faults.categoryName: Hygienic and foreign material contamination risks
faults.what: Lubricant leaking above the product zone; Damaged seal or bearing with visible egress; Gearbox weeping over the conveyor.
conditions: Lubricant leaking above the product zone
Damaged seal or bearing with visible egress
Gearbox weeping over the conveyor
faults.action: Isolate and repair before restart where the leak is over open product, and assess affected product under the site procedure.
faults.benefit: Reduced foreign material contamination risk and reduced sanitation risk.
